subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too want to express my views, not so much to echo the many arguments made in support of or against the budgetary policy, but simply to shed more light on these economic measures which are designed to serve the best interests of Canadians. All Members will agree with that, Mr. Speaker, regardless of their political persuasion.
When the Progressive Conservative Party came into office in 1984, Mr. Speaker, Canada had just pulled through the worst economic crisis of its history, given the means or economic levers it had developed at the time.
We had unprecedented unemployment, interest rates were so high that we start shaking just thinking they might again soar to similar levels, and our indebtedness was beyond imagination.
From Confederation to its centennial, Mr. Speaker, Canada managed to build a railroad from coast to coast, live through two world wars, keep the armed forces abroad with its allies, provide generous financial assistance to developing nations, and set up a network of social programs which are the envy of other industrialized countries. Despite so many advantages, Mr. Speaker, and despite the cost Canadians had to pay to acquire them, our national debt at the time-100 years after Confederation-was under $20-odd billion and debt service charges were less than 5 cents out of every dollar.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians were then known as credible and trustworthy people, and a great many nations enthusiastically chose our country as their meeting place, Montreal's Man and His World, to mark the 100th year of our Confederation at Expo 67.
We were facing a challenging future, Mr. Speaker, and even more prosperous times still lay ahead.
And of course we had a new leader, Mr. Speaker, a man who entertained fresh ideas and came up with a new slogan: The Just Society! That was our challenge to forge ahead. The Liberal Party was euphoric. Nothing was too good.
Mr. Speaker, the first years following 1967 did nothing but give the Liberal Party a few opportunities to show their ability to govern the country, what with the emergence of Quebec's separatism and the energy crisis
The Budget-Mr. Tremblay (Lotbiniere)
which shook the industrialized world during the first years of the Liberal Trudeau government.
Already at that time, Mr. Speaker, it was clear the Liberal Party was not going to be impressed with such trifles. Proud of their century-old history, they owed it to themselves to overcome what could then be viewed as hickups from a handful of intellectuals trying to get attention. Rapidly arrogance set in, and it fueled the rise of Quebec nationalism which almost led to this country's break up during the 1980 referendum. What happened on the constitutional level also happened on the economic level. After a very bad reaction to the first oil crisis, the then Government was about to do the same thing when the second came, so that in the space of 10 years rather than 100, Mr. Speaker, that is from 1975 to 1984, the national debt grew at an appalling rate to nearly $200 billion. The inflation rate clearly showed the then Government lost control of the economy. The unemployment rate reached an all-time high, and even the computers refused to believe we could have such interest rates! That was the legacy left by the Liberal Party!
During those ten years, Mr. Speaker, from 1974 to 1984, the Liberal Government was literally bent on destroying, to put it mildly, what had been built by our ancestors over the previous 110 years. In those ten years, we went through a period of federal-provincial fighting and as you will remember, Mr. Speaker, Quebec even came close to leaving Confederation. We experienced a worsening of the international political climate, first with France which severed most of its economic relations with Canada. And because of France's leadership in Europe, that dispute with France caused a general slowing down of European investment in general.
On the military level, we experienced a period of stagnation that caused us to seriously lag behind in our commitments to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, NATO, so that today the effort needed to fill that gap has become phenomenal if not impossible.
Similarly, following repeated confrontations, our relations with the United States which are our most important economic partner had so soured that we had become increasingly concerned about relying on this vital market for our economy. Such is the legacy of the Liberal Party, Mr. Speaker! In 1974, we were faced with a yearly budgetary surplus of nearly $700 million-imagine that!-which in 1984, some ten years later, had turned

May 9, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Tremblay (Lotbiniere)
into a yearly budgetary deficit of $38.3 billion. What a change, Mr. Speaker!
The economic situation we inherited at the time from the Liberal Party was in such a state of degradation that even the Liberal Party would not and could not govern this country any longer, Mr. Speaker. Our first real challenge was to try and govern this country while trying to curb the deficit, a challenge we have met head-on. Not only have we managed to curb the deficit four years in a row, but at the same time we have used economic leverage to make sure that Canada would enjoy the highest economic growth rate of all the industralized nations except Japan. That is extraordinary too!
During these past four years, we have created over
1,300,000	jobs. Yet, Mr. Speaker, we have not had an easy time. Unfortunately, in spite of our performance, the burden resulting from the debt legacy of 1984 was such that we would have needed all the conditions which would have made favourable and perfectly coordinated economic policies possible.
As we know and as you know, Mr. Speaker, inflation has always been and remains one of the most extremely unpredictable and sensitive factors whose quickly growing pressures can soon cancel out all the benefits resulting from economic growth.
The only true and efficient way to control short term and medium term inflation is through an interest rate policy.
On the other hand, it was clear that maintaining high interest levels would reduce proportionately the Government's margin of operation which was extremely limited, in view of the historic past and the legacy left to us. That is precisely the problem which the current Budget is addressing, Mr. Speaker. This Budget has been put together in such a way as to bring down interest rates to more acceptable levels. And one the cornerstones of this Budget is the sales tax reform.
The existing sales tax which is levied at the manufacturing level is one of the key elements of our strategy aimed at preserving our social programs so important to Canadian men and women and guaranteeing once and for all a sustainable economic growth. The current sales tax produces the revenues needed by the government to finance its essential programs.
This tax has serious flaws. It is hidden from consumer, unfair and damaging to our economy. That's how! Moreover, it's the only tax in industrialized countries which favours imports over domestically produced goods. Think about it. This tax is a total nonsense. In fact, the tax levied on goods produced in Canada is, on average, a third higher than the tax on competitive imported goods. That makes no sense at all! That tax is penalizing Canadians. It represents a significant handicap to our Canadians producers, on the domestic market of course, but also on international markets. That is so obvious!
Right now, the federal sales tax is directly levied on only one third of all goods and services consumed by Canadians. In most instances, services are tax-free, which is advantageous to the well-off Canadians, Mr. Speaker, since those are the people who consume relatively more services.
Again, the existing sales tax is not such a reliable source of revenue for the government. Over the years, the tax system was the subject of many tax avoidance provisions, an assortment of special provisions and administrative interpretations, as well as an increasing number of legal actions by the taxpayers. So, the tax system being a major investment to economic growth, Mr. Speaker, the present government has decided to give this problem top priority and will try to resolve the matter through a sales tax reform. The existing sales tax will be replaced by the Goods and Services Tax on January 1, 1991. The new tax, at a rate of 9 per cent, will be applied on the vast majority of goods and services consumed in Canada.
However, and that is particularly important, basic groceries, prescription drugs and medical devices will not be taxed. Similarly, Mr. Speaker, residential rents, child care services, legal aid and most health, dental and educational services will be exempt as well as loans, mortgages and life insurance premiums. Special steps will be taken to minimize compliance costs for small businesses since, as we all know, small- and mediumsized businesses are the key sector in our economy.
Mr. Speaker, at 9 percent, the new tax will generate enough revenues to replace, not "add to", the present federal sales tax, including the additional revenue it will produce pursuant to the budget. The new tax will also allow further income tax reductions for average households. Finally, it will fund a new sales tax credit which will be considerably more generous than the present one. This refundable credit will be paid out quarterly,
May 9, 1989

the first payment to be made before the coming into effect of the new tax. The government's aim is to ensure that families who earn less than $30,000 a year will be better off after the sales tax reform than before.
Mr. Speaker, help will also be given to home buyers, since this too is a key sector of our economy. As is often said, when construction is booming, so is the economy. In fact, homebuyers who may have trouble finding an affordable house as a result of the tax reform will receive assistance.
At the present time, the consumer has no way of knowing whether the price of the item he buys includes or not a hidden federal sales tax. With the new tax, the consumer will know exactly how much goods and services tax he is paying, which means that it will be easier for him to buy sensibly. In this respect, the goods and services tax is similar to the provincial retail sales tax.
The sales tax reform will provide major economic benefits for Canada. By removing the federal sales tax from the production of goods and services, it will lead to higher investment and improved productivity. There will be greater domestic output and higher real incomes for Canadians.
Strengthening Canada's international competitiveness and eliminating existing biases in favour of imports will encourage Canadian production and help create jobs for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the estimated economic gains as a result of federal sales tax reform will be around $9 billion annually, gains that will be enjoyed by all sectors of the economy and all regions of this country. Sales tax reform will also bring more fairness, a more equitable sharing of the tax burden. It will make federal sales tax fairer and more visible to consumers. It will establish a more stable foundation upon which the Government can maintain essential public services and manage effectively the problem of Canada's debt.
I was listening to the previous speakers who said that in four years we had almost doubled or at least substantially increased the deficit the Liberal Government had left us in 1984. That is what I call irresponsible, Mr. Speaker.
I referred earlier to the state of euphoria in the Liberal Party when they came back in 1967, but now they
The Budget-Mr. Tremblay (Lotbiniere)
are being totally irresponsible. Mr. Speaker, with a population of about 26 million, how do we reduce an annual debt of $ 38.3 billion? How do we do that without touching the sancrosanct principle of universality of our social programs and without cutting into any of the expenditures initiated by the Liberal Party? No, no cut backs! We had to accept the deficit because a Government has no choice but to accept the economic situation it is left by its predecessor. But that isn't what the Liberal Party wanted.
They consider it their prerogative to create debt, but we Conservatives are not allowed to do that. We can't touch anything! That is the legacy they left us. As I said earlier. Mr. Speaker, four consecutive years of reducing the debt is a first in Canada's history. And I may recall that when the Liberals came to power, with the advent of the Just Society, less than 5 cents of every dollar was spent to pay the interest on the debt. Today it is 35 cents and in 1984 it was 31 cents. Once again, all the decisions we have made have an impact on various sectors, and the problem is how to manage debt reduction.
With this Budget's help, however, we will not only maintain our credibility as a Government that manages the interests of this country as they should be managed, we will also be able to bring interest rates down, which is perhaps the most crucial problem today, and thus accelerate reduction of the debt.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I respect the hon. gentleman's position in this House as a Member of Parliament since he was put here by a majority of the constituents in his riding. However, if his constituents heard what he was saying this afternoon in the House, I think that they would be very ashamed of his representation.
The debate before us concerns the Budget. Yet in his remarks he pulled out the problems of separatism and the problems concerning the referendum. He ran down the former Prime Minister, the greatest Prime Minister in the history of Canada, who is not here to defend himself. He talked about former Prime Minister Trudeau being bent on destroying the country.
In my riding I have constituents from over 50 different countries. Practically every one of them says what a great

May 9, 1989
The Budget-Mr, Tremblay (Lotbiniere)
country Canada is. They say: "We are so pleased that we have found ourselves in this country".
Who built the country to that stage if not previous Liberal Governments and previous Prime Ministers such as Pierre Elliott Trudeau?
The Hon. Member talked about the former Prime Minister's reputation. When I was a Member here previously for five years, I had the pleasure of representing Canada in Madrid at the Human Rights Conference, in England and other countries. Members of Parliament would come to me and say: "Mr. Flis, you people are so lucky to have a Prime Minister such as Mr. Trudeau".
The Hon. Member has stood up and in his remarks on the Budget lowered the greatness of our former Prime Minister. I am sure that his constituents will be quite ashamed of his representation.
The Hon. Member talked about the differences among the provinces. Pierre Elliott Trudeau believed in a strong central Government. He did not give in to the whims of every little region in the country. He believed in what was good for the country as a whole.
If the Government of the Hon. Member has such a great rapport with all the provinces why are not most of the provinces supporting the federal sales tax brought in by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson)? Why are three provinces objecting to the Meech Lake Accord if his Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Government have such a great rapport with the provinces?
I am trying to bring the hon. gentleman back to the debate before us and not have him talk about separatism and the referendum. It was thanks to the former Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau that we have today a united Canada.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I understand that members of the Liberal Party praise former Prime Minister Trudeau and will continue to do so because he is indeed the one who made it possible for that bunch of nincompoops to sit with him for more than sixteen years. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, they will glorify him.
Now, I personally would not wish to denigrate him, because we must render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's. But what do you want, politics is also part of government, and the Budget is also part of politics. So
in that way, it is a whole and all those policies had an effect, unfortunately a harmful effect on Canada's development. It is true that Canada remains a country with some credibility because the people see to it every four years. At some point, they had enough and made a radical change because we were literally headed for bankruptcy. The Hon. Member says, "Look, Mr. Trudeau still believes in a strong Canada-" We certainly know that; he even took the trouble to travel here from Montreal, to go to the Senate Chamber and again give his vision of Canada-an outdated vision. How can one support such a former Prime Minister who to boost his ego-imagine-repatriates the Constitution without the agreement of the Province of Quebec, one of this country's founding nations? Why do you want to pay tribute to such a Prime Minister! And when you say that in fact there are three provinces opposed to the Meech Lake Accord, that is wrong, unless you are a Liberal, perhaps!
None of the Premiers is intelligently opposed to the Accord. They are for the Accord but want it improved. That is the reason for their opposition, because they want to repair not just a mistake but an aberration in Canadian history. Imagine! What province do you come from? From an English-speaking province. If your province had not signed the agreement in 1982, would you be so proud of the man who was then your Prime Minister? Well, I am from the Province of Quebec and I feel that our rights were violated and ridiculed to satisfy the Liberal Party's own ego so that it could continue to spend and leave us a $38-billion debt, not in 100 years but in one year, twice as much as in the previous 100 years. That is what your former Prime Minister and your Liberal Party did!
Yes, you may well leave this House, this honourable Chamber which is entitled to honourable remarks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me first to commend the Hon. Member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Tremblay), an outspoken member who is expressing the beliefs of Canadians and his constituents. The Hon. Member for Lotbiniere was re-elected with a five-fold majority, and this is quite an achievement we recognize.
The Hon. Member opposite suggests his constituents were not proud of him, but I rather believe the Hon. Member for Lotbiniere has been active enough during these last four years to get re-elected by five times his previous majority.
May 9, 1989

The Budget-Ms. Phinney
Mr. Speaker, I was listening to his speech on the federal sales tax. Although I am in total agreement with him, I know the Hon. Member for Lotbiniere emphasized the antiquity of the federal sales tax. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the federal sales tax is entitled to its old age security pension because it is turning 65 this year.
We also know the new tax proposed for 1991 is already in place in 48 nations around the world and it works very well.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Lotbiniere, in view of our antiquated federal sales tax system and the example set in 48 nations, doesn't he feel that indeed, here in Canada, that new tax will be most valuable not only to the country as a whole but to every Canadian?

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank and I commend the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Vincent) who, in his capacity as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, ensured that this Budget is in line with realities Mr. Speaker, because we have international economic relations as well as political ones. Canada must consider adjusting to what is going on around us.
As I said, Mr. Speaker we are essentially an exporting nation. We export some 85 per cent of almost everything we produce. It is therefore vital to look at what is going on around us. The current sales tax is recessive, hidden, unfair, and it does not bring the Government adequate support.
With this new type of tax on the other hand, and as I said this is a replacement rather than something added-on to what already exists, we are going to do-away with the old tax and are going to tax at a much more normal and fairer rate. But now Canadians will know what they are buying, and also a widened tax base will allow the Government much more sustained revenues, as I said earlier to the Hon. Member from the English speaking provinces, so that Canada may maintain its vital economic credibility.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions and comments are now over. The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Phinney) for debate.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Budget has deeply shaken my faith. I always believed in Canada as the tomorrow land, a golden land, a gift to an inherently decent people: Canadians. A gift of abundance that needed only to be administered by a fair and hopefully wise group of legislators. But this Budget is a parody of fairness. It panders to and protects the privileged and the profit takers and hurts those who are struggling to make a decent living. It abandons the needy and misdirects the public with its bafflegab.
What is most frustrating is to see the Hon. Minister introduce the Budget with the same amount of dignity one would accord to a new brand of toothpaste or mouth wash entering the market-place. After introducing his Budget at the press conference, he has launched a crass media blitz. A silver dollar rolling on to the screen should be the first signal that Canadians are about to get the run- around from this Government once again.
Thirty seconds later we are no wiser about the content of the Budget than we are about the contents of toothpaste. Once again, our pockets are lighter as we are made to pay for this ridiculous exercise.
What is truly galling about these commercials is the implied threat that if we do not deal with the debt now we risk losing our social programs in the near future.
The Finance Minister has already attacked those social programs by completely stopping the federal Government's support to the unemployment insurance program, and with the claw- back clause on senior pensions and family allowances. He is fighting the deficit by broadening the taxation, rather than trimming the operation costs and eliminating unnecessary expenditures.
It adds up to a trim in spending of $3.5 billion, new taxes and assorted other measures of extracting funds from the people of $10.6 billion. It is the Government versus the Canadian people and as the score indicates, in this Budget the people are clearly losing.
The UIC rolls will shrink, the Minister tells us, and the funds will be earmarked for retraining. What are we training them for? Where are the jobs? The Minister cannot predict that there will be jobs. He cannot predict where those jobs will be. If he does not know what and where, then how will he know what they need to be trained for? Providing Canadians with sketchy, questionable training and not providing jobs, dumping them from the UIC rolls straight on to the welfare line, is this the present Government's idea of progress?

May 9, 1989
The Budget-Ms. Phinney
This country has been built on the free enterprise system. The people I represent on Elamilton Mountain believe in a strong private sector and jobs, good jobs. They want to see us using our resources wisely, creating jobs through research and marketing, not squandering our precious resources on whoever wants them for a quick buck. Canada spends less on research and development than almost any western country. That is a scandal. We have an embarrassment of riches and all this Government does is give them away. What about creating wealth? What about focusing those resources and encouraging the growth of industry that our children will benefit from. Where are the guidelines that demand a partnership with Canadians? It should be considered a privilege to do business in Canada. There is a skilled labour force, an abundance of resources and access to transportation.
We have a stable democracy. We are next door to one of the largest, most lucrative markets in the world. Yet foreign investors dump large chunks of capital into real estate and commercial development in this country. They sit and wait for the equity to build and their money is as safe as it would be in a bank, reducing Canadians to the status of tenants in their own land.
Where are the jobs that are created from this type of investment? When did obligation and accountability go out of vogue? Why have we not learned from the economic initiatives of European and Pacific Rim countries, which have learned that research gives a country a competitive edge and that aggressive market strategies provide the mission statement for a healthy nation. We are faced in this country with a gap between the haves and the have nots that is accelerating at an unnerving rate. Witness the need for food banks in our major cities, a need that hardly existed five years ago. The victims, single parent families, usually headed by women, and the casualties of plant shutdowns, where is the hope for them?
The Budget is not solely an administrative tool any longer. Today, more than ever, it should be a tool for social justice. Skilfully wielded by a person with vision, it has the power to achieve greatness, to create wealth and opportunity and the social justice that Canadians demand. However, in the hands of a Government with no social conscience, the Budget also has the power to create despair. For the single mother in Toronto, the fisherman in the Atlantic provinces, the smoke stack
industries in our cities, the underfunded research centres and universities, where is the thoughtful consideration of their future? They are the heart and the essence of Canada.
I remember when Canadians talked about a just society, when we were admired for our quality of life and of opportunity, and not solely for our viability as an economic unit. Canadians have a sense of fairness that extends far beyond our borders. According to a recent poll, 86 per cent of Canadians believe Canada has a moral duty to assist the developing world. In the Third World, Canada means hope. Canada is a helping hand in times of crisis, a partner in long-term programs that help people help themselves.
With this Budget I fear Canada will be known instead for hypocrisy. While the globe-trotting Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) pretends to be a friend of the developing world, this Government has cut the foreign aid budget by $1.8 billion. It has turned its back on the most vulnerable people on earth, on those who go hungry, who have no access to basic medical care, no roof over their heads and no school for their children. Is this what Canada stands for? Is this the uncaring face we show the rest of the world?
Let us not forget the economic cost of these vicious cuts in foreign aid. Canada relies on its export markets. By turning our backs on the developing world, we throw Canadians out of work. I quote from a speech by Ivan Head, the President of the International Development Research Centre to the Canadian Club of Hamilton recently: "The economic downturn in the southern hemisphere in the past seven years has led to the loss of
130,000	Canadian jobs and at least $24 billion in export revenues".
This Government must pull its head out of the sand. The world is becoming more interdependent every day. By slashing foreign aid, we reduce Canada's stature in the world community. We undermine the goodwill that is so important in expanding our export markets. We ignore the threat to the planet's environment. Worst of all, we ignore the suffering of millions of our fellow human beings. The cost of progress must always be balanced against the quality of life. Canadians recognize this. We have always paid the premium. Historically, we have always decided that the cost of being Canadian is not too high but, indeed, a bargain for the freedoms and privileges we have enjoyed.
May 9, 1989

We Liberals measure our success much differently than do Tories, that much is evident. The Tories look for comparisons with the giant economic unit to the south. We Liberals, on the other hand, measure success by finding ways to meet the needs of Canadians now and in the future.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions or comments? the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to the comments of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Phinney) and felt compelled to make a couple of comments and ask her a question.
The Hon. Member's speech contained the mandatory criticism, of course, criticizing the expenditure reductions in the Budget and criticizing the tax increases. She went on to accuse the Government of hypocrisy and, yet, in the Hon. Member's speech she criticized the Government for expenditure reductions. At the same time, she suggested the Government has not gone far enough in chopping the fat out and in reducing expenditures. I find the Hon. Member's message rather contradictory.
I believe she went on to say that we paid a premium for being Canadians. I think, if anything, what we have done is mortgaged the future in order to pay for the programs of the past and that is what has led us into this debt problem that we have today, the interest charges on which are consuming so much of our national revenue and which threaten the social programs of tomorrow and, indeed, the future of our children.
I heard the Hon. Member criticize tax increases on the one hand, criticize expenditure reductions on the other. I would like the Hon. Member to say here today what she and her Party would do to meet the problem that we have out there. We will not even bother getting into recriminations about how that debt arose, but let us just talk about addressing the problem today. What would the Hon. Member and her Party do in place of the measures which the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has put forward?

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Liberals have to take any lessons from the Conservatives about the way the Budget has been run. The Conservative Party, our present Government, has doubled the debt in
The Budget-Mr. G. Wilson
the last four years. We have a Budget now that will not cut the deficit and will not cut down on the debt.
I think one thing is apparent to the public, and I have probably 40 or 50 letters from my riding coming in every day explaining how people feel about the Budget. It is the people who have to pay for these cuts, the same people over and over again, those people who can least afford them. I think an example in the Minister's Budget in Brief that we saw the night before the Budget was brought down in the House. It explains the philosophy of this Government when it is talking about the cut in foreign aid and considers it a saving. Savings will amount to $1.8 billion. When we cut the budget to foreign aid, the present Government is calling that a saving. Our Party would not consider it a saving to cut foreign aid by $1.8 billion.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have a question, Mr. Speaker. I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Phinney) whether she feels this Government has the mandate to do some of the things that it proposes to do in the current Budget. For example, does the Government have the mandate to privatize unemployment insurance? The Tories certainly did not talk about privatizing unemployment insurance during the election campaign. Does this Government have the mandate to bring an end to universality? There was no discussion in the campaign about bringing universality to an end. There was no discussion about further severe cuts to the CBC. There is talk now, for example, of perhaps changing the mandate of the CBC as a result of cuts, closing down stations, for example, at Sydney, in Labrador, in Saskatchewan.
Given the rhetoric from this Government during the election campaign, does the Hon. Member feel that this Government has the mandate to do what it is proposing to do?

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think probably it could be argued that the Government does not have the mandate to do what it is proposing. The Government discussed before the election that the Party which managed this country should be given the mandate and the power for another four or five years because they, the Tories, had done such a good job managing the economy over the last five years. As I have already mentioned, that management consisted of doubling the debt over the past four years. The Government asked us to give it the mandate for another five years but unfortunately, as

May 9, 1989
Canadians are learning, the Tories do not deserve this mandate.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Phinney). It has to do with this very, very important area of universality which is pretty basic to the social programs in this country. The Conservative Government will argue that the claw-back of old age security is not an assault on universality. But, in fact, it is.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are wrong.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think there is any doubt that once the Government introduces legislation in a Budget allowing a total claw-back of a social service-

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: From the rich.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -then you have, in fact, the termination of the application of universality.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, they all get a cheque.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It may be $50,000 now but the Finance Minister may decide next year he will reduce that amount to $40,000 or $30,000 or $25,000. Then the old age security becomes a government hand-out or a social welfare payment to the elderly who are retired. That is then the end of universality.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is this a question?

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The question I want to put to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain-and I thank her for her maiden speech if it was her maiden speech. It was her first speech I have listened to in this House. I congratulate her on that and on her election. I want to know whether or not her Party would restore full universality if they were elected at the next election.

subsubtopic: THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, universality is the basic right of all Canadians. At what point will it stop? The Government is saying now $50,000. Next year that amount may be $40,000 and the next year $30,000. It is a basic right of every Canadian to receive their pension and their family allowance.

subsubtopic: PLO MEMBERSHIP IN WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 166-member assembly, the World Health Organization's governing body, began its annual two-week session yesterday. The organization may be taking a very important but divisive vote today. The vote is whether or not to grant full membership to the Palestine Liberation Organization.
Full membership in WHO would automatically allow the PLO to join several other agencies such as the UN Conference on Trade and Development. The United States, which contributes 25 per cent of WHO's yearly budget of $73.8 million, is expected to vote against the PLO because it is not a legitimate state in control of a territory, borders or a government. Admittance to full membership is therefore both undeserved and premature. I am pleased to say that for the same reasons, Canada will also be voting against any move to grant full membership to the PLO.

Mr. Speaker, something is rotten in the State of Michigan. The Detroit garbage incinerator will be completed this month without state-of-the-art pollution controls. The Government has not even lifted a finger to stop or to delay the world's largest incinerator.
This garbage-burning monster is only three miles from the Canadian border but the impact area extends well into Ontario. Sailing in the breeze every year will be sulphur oxides, hydrogen chlorides, arsenic, chromium, mercury, dioxins and furans which could be reduced by imposing the necessary controls. The incinerator will burn 2,000 tonnes of trash each and every day.
May 9, 1989

The Americans say it is too expensive to install better anti-pollution equipment. I say it is much more expensive to affect the health of residents downwind.
The Government should follow the lead of Ontario's Environment Minister. He is showing guts and real commitment by taking the Yankees to court. He is defending our interests. Where is the Government of Canada on this matter?

subtopic: RECOGNITION OF FIVE DISTINGUISHED BUSINESS WOMEN OF ABITIBI-TEMISCAMINGUE
RECOGNITION OF FIVE DISTINGUISHED BUSINESS WOMEN OF ABITIBI-TEMISCAMINGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, women entrepreneurs have finally come of age in Abitibi-Temiscamingue. And to emphasize this fact, the Abitibi-Temiscamingue Chambers of Commerce every year give an award to five women who have made their mark in the business world through their dynamism and outstanding achievements.
I should like to congragulate Diane Raymond, from Ville-Marie, Lise Gendron, from La Sarre, Helene Lagrange, from Rouyn-Noranda, Dolly Lepack, from Val d'Or, and Jocelyne Deshaies, from Amos, the five award winners for 1989 for their tremendous success in the business world. Through these women, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congragulate and thank all the women who are continuously working for the development of our Abitibi-Temiscamingue region.

Mr. Speaker, this past weekend in my riding, two lobster boats became caught in excess silt and were forced to wait until the tide came in before they could come ashore. Events like this should never happen and would never happen if the ports of Prince Edward Island were properly dredged.
The recent Budget is inadequate. It is unacceptable because it does not have sufficient money to keep our harbours safe and our wharfs properly maintained.
The fishery is one of the most important industries in Prince Edward Island. It means approximately $80 million in landed value to the fishermen and totals about $200 million to the Prince Edward Island economy. I urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to think again and to evaluate the effects of his budget on the safety and future of the fishery in Prince Edward Island.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to draw the attention of the Government once again to the crisis of deteriorating roadways, bridges and sewer systems across Canada. One example that portrays this crisis is the fact that more than eight million Canadians live in municipalities that provide no sewage treatment whatsoever.
Municipalities do not have the tax base to address this issue alone but are willing to raise their share of one-third of the cost as are all provincial Governments. The federal Government is not, despite veiled promises made from time to time before the Budget. In the meantime, both the deterioration and the price escalates. It is now $15 billion.
The Federation of Canadian Municipalities has a concrete proposal endorsed by its 1,200-plus members which would help clean up our environment, create
60,000	good paying jobs, reduce the deficit through tax revenue and rebuild the infrastructure of Canada. I call on the Government to enact one positive initiative out of a totally negative and regressive Budget and allocate the $600 million generated from tax increases on gasoline to this plan. It would be a small step toward addressing the issue, but at least it would be a positive step which would improve the quality of life of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Lower St. Lawrence Gaspe Forest Association has just held in the Matapedia Valley its annual convention which had brought together under the same roof some 200 groups more or less directly involved in forestry and the important roles it plays in our daily lives.

May 9, 1989
This year, during the Week of the Tree which will be held between May 7 to 13, each Canadian man and woman should plant a tree and use this period to reflect on the impact forests have on our economy, environment, our health generally, as well as on the conservation of our fauna and water resources.
Contrary to an opinion held much too long, Mr. Speaker, this wealth is not inexhaustible and should be preserved through a well thought out forestry policy so that future generations can enjoy healthy and luxuriant forests.
Today, Mr. Speaker, we are no longer referring to lumbermen but forestry workers who fully deserved admiration and to whom I wish to pay here a special tribute. They are the gardeners who through their professional dedication, will deliver the forests of tomorrow.
Finally, I want to pay a special tribute to the late J. Donat Brule, a great forestry engineer who founded the "Club 4H" on February 20, 1940, in an effort to teach young men and young women the desire to protect trees.

Mr. Speaker, once again we have evidence of the Government being less than candid and indeed untruthful with the Canadian people in respect of the real effects of the trade deal. In today's issue of The Globe and Mail, Galen Weston, food conglomerate chairman and president of Loblaws, says that Canadians should not expect any kind of break at the supermarkets as a result of the Free Trade Agreement.
During the election campaign, the Government promised Canadian families that $85 to $130 would be saved annually by a family of four on their supermarket bills due to cheaper imports as a result of the free trade deal. Instead, we have seen over the last year a 4 per cent hike in grocery prices, the largest increase since the summer of 1987. As a result of the 1989 Budget tax grab, we can expect further food price increases.
Again, we have seen the Government mislead the Canadian consumer and have evidenced the Government's lack of credibility in keeping election promises. Even the corporate friends of the Prime Minister such as Galen Weston are now saying that the Government has misled the people of Canada on the Free Trade Agreement.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT THE CRTC REVIEW CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS
REQUEST THAT THE CRTC REVIEW CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a decision rendered by the CRTC concerning an aspect of telecommunications in Western Quebec does not reflect the reality of the Ottawa area and the services that its people want.
The proposal by Bell Canada is the result of several years of consultations with all the municipalities and local agencies. Bell Canada's proposal, in conjunction with the municipalities, is fair and equitable since it gives Western Quebec the same services as are found on the Ontario side.
We ask, Mr. Speaker, that the CRTC review the proposals and render a decision which truly reflects the situation in Western Quebec.

subtopic: DECLINE IN NUMBER OF FARM BANKRUPTCIES
DECLINE IN NUMBER OF FARM BANKRUPTCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the number of farm bankruptcies declined by 8.2 per cent in 1988, continuing the downward trend established in 1984. Of course, there are many reasons for this positive trend. Ever-improving fiscal management and improvements in prices of some agricultural commodities are two major factors. Major financial support by the federal Government, through stabilization, special grains and drought assistance programs, has also been a major contributor to the improved economic outlook on many of our farms. The economic well-being of our farm families is a concern of all of us. Leadership by the federal Government has and will continue to assist in the continued evolution of a strong agricultural industry in Canada.
May 9, 1989

subtopic: SEVENTH SQUASH TOURNAMENT BETWEEN MP'S AND THE PRESS

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SEVENTH SQUASH TOURNAMENT BETWEEN MP'S AND THE PRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the star athletes of the parliamentary media and the ordinary sportsmen of the House of Commons have just held their Seventh Squash Tournament.
Although our opponents had obviously been training hard for a long time, they barely held on to the cup in this tournament between the media people and the elected representatives.
Since 1984, the tally is: MP's 5, Media 2.
I congratulate them, but our day will come. See you next time.

subsubtopic: TRAIN TO WAKEFIELD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to talk about the financial contribution of the federal government to the proposed tourist train between Hull and Wakefield.
As a result of unrelenting efforts on the part of the community, particularly representatives of the three city involved, Hull, Hull-Ouest and La Peche, which have bought the railway infrastructure between Hull and Wakefield, Quebec has granted $1.4 million to this project which will bring in $17 million in revenue and create about 124 jobs.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the federal and provincial governments have been playing ping-pong with the tourist train proposal, and that unwarranted delay could jeopardize the project scheduled to start in May 1990.
Consequently, I insist that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion speed up the analysis so that the project sponsors can get an answer before the end of May of this year, of course, Mr. Speaker. I do hope the Hon. Member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle will support my request.

subsubtopic: ONTARIO GOVERNMENT'S EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my constituents are upset about high interest rates that are a result of government debt and inflation. Our Government has attacked this debt. We are told interest rates are high to fight the ravages of inflation. Westerners ask, what inflation? Inflation in Alberta is not out of control, but it is in Toronto, and we are all paying for it. Another irresponsible Liberal Government is spending like a drunken sailor at a time when its economy is booming. Its excessive government spending and deficit financing is fueling inflation and driving up interest rates to the detriment of Canadians in western Canada and in other regions.
Our Government is taking bold initiatives to fight the debt. What is the Peterson Government doing? While we trimmed 10,000 civil service jobs, Ontario has increased its civil service by 7,000. While we cut salaries and spending by 25 per cent, the Ontario Government increased spending by 24 per cent. When we cut administrative costs by 48.3 per cent, the Ontario Government's comparable costs increased by 25 per cent. Westerners are saying, enough is enough.

subsubtopic: CLOSING OF ROCKET RANGE AT CHURCHILL, MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for years now Canadians have known that the ozone layer, sheltering the earth from the sun's harmful rays, is at risk. Canadians should also know that we have one of the finest research stations for monitoring that ozone layer right here in Canada. In Churchill, Manitoba, we have what is considered the finest northern rocket range station in the free world for studying the ozone layer. The Manitoba launcher is praised by American and Canadian scientists alike. I quote one American scientist who has said:
It is the best location for such research.
In addition, Churchill's launching pads are indoors and heated, essential for winter launching. However, in 1985, the Canadian Government decided to shut down the Churchill rocket range by 1992.

May 9, 1989
Oral Questions
Since 1985, however, we have discovered the need for rocket research in order to better understand and monitor the ozone layer. Since 1985, the United States itself has doubled its annual number of rocket launches. This year there have been four NASA launches in Churchill. Given the renewed interest by the North American scientific community in the use of rocket launchers, I would call upon the Government to reconsider its decision to close down the Churchill rocket range.

subsubtopic: MR. ROGER LAGASSE'S BICYCLE TOUR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, today I would like to salute Mr. Roger Lagasse and to wish him success on the bicycle tour he plans to do across Canada. As you know, Mr. Lagasse, a long-standing member of the New Democratic Party, wants to succeed Mr. Broad-bent. It was reported today in The Citizen that Mr. Lagasse is planning this cross-Canada bicycle tour to make himself known and to collect funds for his campaign. Himself and his NDP colleagues are strong supporters of development and environmental issues as well as other issues. I hope Mr. Lagasse will complete his tour on time and will give an example of courage, honesty and professional ethics to all other candidates who, like him, wish to participate in the leadership campaign.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: STUDENT FARES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, over the next few weeks, thousands of Canadian university students will criss-cross this vast country in search of summer employment opportunities. All Members of this House are well aware of the cost of travel in Canada and should ask, how can university students carry this burden of travel expense? The student stand-by fare to travel from Nova Scotia to British Columbia is $460, $50 more than the seat-sale price. Surely, Canada's major airlines can give students a better deal on empty seats. I call upon Air Canada and Canadian International Airlines to give students a break.

subsubtopic: ENCOURAGEMENT OF TRADE WITH POLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the Paris Club, of which Canada is a member, held a special session on Poland's substantial foreign debt. For over seven years, the western world has been using economic sanctions to push for reforms that they believed would enable Poland to salvage its own economy independently. The legalization of Solidarity has motivated the United States, France and Germany to accept in principle some of the responsibility for trying to ease the burden of debt that has crippled Poland for so long.
We are pleased to have the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Poland's People's Republic, Mr. Olechowski, with us in Canada to discuss the developments that have occurred in his country and the ways and means in which we can facilitate freer trade between our countries. Poland is seeking to reschedule its foreign debt, and we should be generous in our approach by encouraging joint ventures, promoting investment and increasing Polish imports to Canada. We look forward to the elections in June as a symbol that Poland is moving in the right direction towards economic stability and greater freedom for the people of Poland.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: OLD AGE PENSIONS-UNIVERSALITY PRINCIPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. It used to be that Canadians in this country who worked for 45 years and helped build our country were entitled as a matter of citizenship to the old age pension. But now more and more Canadians are telling Members of Parliament, why bother planning for retirement when the Conservative Party can change the rules at any time? To show the injustice of the Minister's proposals on old age pensions, I want to use his formula, which he cutely calls CPI-3. Using his formula, will the Minister confirm that 55 year-old Canadians whose incomes are currently $25,000, as a result of inflation will have their old-age pension taxed back at age 80? Will he confirm that 45 year-old Canadians whose incomes are $18,000 will, as a
May 9, 1989

result of the same formula, have their old age pension taxed back at age 80?
What is that, Mr. Speaker, if not the end of universality of our social programs?

subsubtopic: OLD AGE PENSIONS-UNIVERSALITY PRINCIPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think Canadians know from the many improvements that we have brought into the retirement savings system over the last four years that we are veiy, very much committed to a very responsible and broad retirement savings system in Canada. We have improved the Canada pension plan system. We have improved the rules on vesting and on portability and part-time pensions so that many more people can be eligible for pensions. They can also move those pensions and take them with them when they change jobs.
We have changed the rules on Registered Retirement Income Funds, again to give people more flexibility on the investment of their retirement savings when they reach age 71. Our commitment is very clear.
What the Hon. Member is attempting to do with his question is to draw very unfair conclusions. He knows that we made changes when we brought in the CPI-mi-nus-three formula in 1985. In 1987 we proposed changes that raised thresholds for people who were affected by that through an increase in the low-income threshold. subsubtopic: ADDITION OF HAZARDOUS PRODUCTS TO FUELS-MINISTER'S POSITION

A charge has been laid, and it was in the general scope of the transportation of dangerous goods under an Act of Canada and the accord between the United States and Canada.
